release_note: Batch 5 adds six hidden optional flowering/spikelet character groups with direct source-page citations to Diggs et al. (1999). Evidence only ranks positively, never excludes or promotes a specimen ID. Setaria bristles, Arundo lemma hairs and Phragmites rachilla hairs are separated.

characters.label: Leaf blade shape
characters.hint: Look at a fresh, expanded blade. V-folded and inward-rolled leaves are different. Drying or drought may change the apparent shape.

characters.label: Leaf width
characters.hint: Measure a fresh blade near its widest point. Ranges are approximate and can overlap; flatten curled leaves when practical.

characters.label: Leaf tip
characters.hint: Examine a mature intact tip, not one torn by mowing or grazing.

characters.label: Blade edge
characters.hint: Observe under a hand lens. Some grass edges can cut skin; don't drag fingers across them.

characters.label: Leaf midrib
characters.hint: Look along the center of the blade, separate from its edge.

characters.label: Veins, ribs & grooves
characters.hint: Look at both sides of a fresh blade with a hand lens. Parallel veins are common to grasses; a white center vein, raised single keel, paired pale grooves and many lengthwise ribs are different structures.

options.label: Two pale grooves beside the midrib

characters.label: Leaf blade hairs
characters.hint: Use a hand lens if needed. Check whether hairs occur mostly at the base or across the blade. Collar and sheath hairs are separate.

characters.label: Leaf base / sheath
characters.hint: Look where a blade joins its sheath. Ears (auricles) are separate from ligules.

characters.label: Ligule height
characters.hint: Open the blade–sheath junction to measure the true ligule, not adjacent collar hairs.

characters.label: Ligule edge
characters.hint: Find the inner papery flap or hair fringe. A ragged edge differs from fine hairs growing off its margin.

characters.label: Leaf sheath opening
characters.hint: Check a fresh leaf. Closed sheaths sometimes split as they dry.

characters.label: Leaf sheath shape and feel
characters.hint: Examine the sheath surrounding the stem, not the exposed blade.

characters.label: How the stem grows
characters.hint: Follow a stem, not just a drooping leaf. Knee-bent stems bend at a real joint; decumbent stems lie low but turn upright at the end. All extra answers are optional.

characters.label: Surface runners and rooting
characters.hint: A stolon is a separate creeping horizontal stem with nodes. A low flowering stem that roots at one joint is not necessarily a stolon.

characters.label: Underground stems
characters.hint: A rhizome has real stem nodes and scale leaves. Don't call ordinary roots or a short crown a rhizome, and do not dig plants where collection is restricted.

characters.label: Stem base and crown
characters.hint: Look at an attached plant base. Hard, knotty perennial crowns differ from long creeping runners; large cane stems are a separate clue.

characters.label: Other stem clues
characters.hint: Uncommon features can help with look-alikes, but verify them on the same grass as the other observations.

characters.label: Node hairs and gland rings
characters.hint: Examine an actual joint on the stem. Hairs at the ligule or leaf collar are different from node hairs. Some species vary by plant and season.

options.label: Hairs on a surface runner's joints

characters.label: Florets in one spikelet
characters.hint: Check one mature spikelet with a hand lens. Several tiny florets can sit inside one spikelet, not on separate seedhead branches.

characters.label: How spikelets sit
characters.hint: Follow the actual little spikelets on a flowering branch: a stalked/stalkless pair differs from separate rows or one-sided branches.

options.label: On one side of a branch

characters.label: Outer glumes
characters.hint: Look at the two outer spikelet scales, not the leaf sheath. A hand lens helps with small veins.

characters.label: Lemma surface
characters.hint: Check a floral scale itself for hairs, wrinkles, reddish marks or shininess. A hairy flower stalk is not a hairy lemma.

characters.label: Awns on the lemma
characters.hint: A true awn grows from a floral scale. Setaria's surrounding bristles are different structures. Some species vary.

characters.label: Bristles and floral hairs
characters.hint: Check where hairs attach: under the spikelet, on the rachilla, on the lemma, or on the stalk of a reduced partner.

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1334, Triticum aestivum species account
evidence.note: The wheat lemma may be awnless or bear an awn reaching 150 mm or more. Presence/absence varies by cultivar and spikelet.

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1334, Triticum aestivum species account
evidence.note: Solitary spikelets alternate on opposite sides of the zigzag unbranched spike axis; choose 'two rows' based on the full axis, not two rows on one raceme face.

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1252, Bromus catharticus species account with immediately preceding species key
evidence.note: The exact Bromus species key differentiates sharply keeled rescue brome lemmas that are awnless or have a short 1–3 mm apical awn.

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1252, Bromus catharticus species account with immediately preceding species key
evidence.note: Rescue brome species account describes glabrous spikelets, including hairless glumes; absence of hair is not evidence of another spikelet feature.

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1252, Bromus catharticus species account with immediately preceding species key
evidence.note: Species account reports spikelets glabrous; optional 'hairless or smooth' refers to lemma surface, not lack of a strong lemma keel.

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1253, Bromus tectorum species account with immediately preceding species key
evidence.note: The regional Bromus key gives cheatgrass lemma awns about 12–18 mm long; these are true awns arising between the two lemma teeth.

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1253, Bromus tectorum species account with immediately preceding species key
evidence.note: Variety tectorum has soft-hairy lemmas, while var. glabratus has glabrous or rough, essentially hairless lemmas. Do not use hair presence as an absolute exclusion.

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1312, Poa annua species account

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1312, Poa arachnifera species account
evidence.note: Texas bluegrass pistillate lemmas have long cilia on the keel and a basal cobwebby tuft; staminate lemmas have subtler cilia and basal hairs. Sex determines intensity.

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1253, Buchloe dactyloides (now Bouteloua dactyloides) species account
evidence.note: Buffalograss has two-flowered staminate spikelets but one-flowered pistillate spikelets; dioecy and occasional monoecy prevent a single rigid count.
evidence.taxon_crosswalk: Buchloe dactyloides in Diggs 1999 = Bouteloua dactyloides in the Hays learner.

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1268, Eleusine indica species account

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1268, Eleusine indica species account
evidence.note: Goosegrass has awnless spikelets according to the exact species treatment; do not confuse sharp glume/lemma tips with true awns.

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1314, Polypogon viridis species account

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1306, Paspalum notatum species account

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1274, exact Erioneuron pilosum species account treatment

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1274, exact Erioneuron pilosum species account treatment

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1290, exact Nassella leucotricha species account treatment

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1318, exact Secale cereale species account treatment

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1318, exact Secale cereale species account treatment
evidence.note: Regional Flora explicitly says its narrow glumes are apparently one-nerved; this is tentative positive evidence rather than a mandatory exclusion.

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1318, exact Secale cereale species account treatment

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1330, exact Tridens texanus species account treatment
evidence.note: Texas tridens has about 6–12 florets per spikelet.

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1330, exact Tridens texanus species account treatment
evidence.note: Lemmas are pubescent on their nerves below the middle; inspect with magnification.

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1330, exact Tridens texanus species account treatment

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1332, exact Tripsacum dactyloides species account treatment

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1332, exact Tripsacum dactyloides species account treatment

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1335, exact Urochloa texana species account treatment

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1306, exact Paspalum floridanum species account treatment

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1252, exact Bromus pubescens species account treatment

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1252, exact Bromus pubescens species account treatment
evidence.note: Species explicitly places dense pubescence on lemma floral scales.

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1256, exact Chloris cucullata species account treatment

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1258, exact Chloris verticillata species account treatment
evidence.note: Tumble windmill grass has a fertile basal floret plus one slightly inflated sterile floret, not multiple fertile florets.

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1258, exact Chloris virgata species account treatment

Owner's temporary same-organ regional Diggs preference retains 'two'; rare 3-floret several state HELD pending specimen-specific sex/age and UI handling, not erased.

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1288, exact Muhlenbergia lindheimeri species account treatment

evidence.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, printed p. 1290, exact Muhlenbergia schreberi species account treatment

evidence.note: Strict separately recognized Bothriochloa longipaniculata: TRUE FERTILE LEMMA awn 11.8–15.5 mm in Scrivanti p.37; USDA reports 10–18 mm awn bending near its base. BENT does not prove TWISTED; do NOT assign bent_twisted. Historical Diggs (1999) B. laguroides subsp. torreyana pooled distinct taxa, so do not transfer that broad concept blindly.

evidence.note: Strict modern B. torreyana: one fertile SESSILE spikelet paired with a PEDICELLATE/stalked partner. The partner is not necessarily reduced; only paired is supported. Historical Diggs B. laguroides subsp. torreyana groups names now separated.

evidence.note: LOWER glume rudimentary or absent; UPPER glume one-veined, 1–2 mm. Do not imply BOTH glumes one-veined. Surrounding involucre BRISTLES are not lemma awns. Historic Pennisetum setaceum name and introduced ornamental context retained.

evidence.note: LOWER glume alone one-veined (1–1.3 mm); UPPER glume 5–7-veined. Historical Cenchrus incertus name included in current species concept. Burr spines are NOT lemma awns; positive clue attaches to identified lower glume only.
